clinicalPearls: Caused by Trichostrongylus species, small nematodes chiefly of herbivores, with human infection common in rural farming communities of Asia, the Middle East and elsewhere
Acquired by ingesting infective larvae on contaminated vegetables and greens, in contrast to the skin-penetrating route of true hookworms
Most infections are light and asymptomatic; heavier burdens cause abdominal pain, diarrhoea, nausea and, occasionally, mild anaemia
Peripheral eosinophilia is common and may be the clue that prompts stool examination
The eggs resemble hookworm eggs but are larger with more pointed ends, and can be mistaken for them on routine microscopy
Treatment is with a benzimidazole anthelmintic such as albendazole, which is highly effective
Prevention relies on adequate sanitation, avoiding use of animal manure on food crops and washing or cooking vegetables
reference.pathophysiology: Trichostrongylus species are small nematodes that normally parasitise the intestines of sheep, goats, cattle and other herbivores. Eggs passed in the faeces of these animals develop in soil into infective larvae that contaminate low-growing vegetables and herbage. Humans acquire infection by ingesting these larvae rather than through skin penetration. In the small intestine the larvae mature into adult worms that attach superficially to the mucosa, where light infections cause little harm. Heavier worm burdens produce localised mucosal irritation and inflammation with abdominal symptoms and diarrhoea, and chronic infection can contribute to mild blood and protein loss and anaemia. Eggs shed in the faeces return to the soil to continue the cycle, sustained by both animal reservoirs and human contamination.
additionalDifferentials: Hookworm infection (Ancylostoma or Necator), given similar eggs
Strongyloidiasis and other intestinal nematode infection
Irritable bowel syndrome or functional dyspepsia
Other causes of eosinophilia with gastrointestinal symptoms
Coeliac disease or another cause of mild malabsorption
additionalInvestigations: Stool microscopy for ova and parasites, with concentration methods
Careful egg morphometry to distinguish from hookworm eggs
Full blood count for eosinophilia and anaemia
Larval culture of stool to confirm the species where required
Repeat stool sampling in light infection
Dietary and occupational history of exposure to livestock and raw vegetables
redFlags: Significant anaemia in heavy or chronic infection
Symptoms unresponsive to appropriate anthelmintic therapy
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is excellent, as infection is usually mild and clears readily with anthelmintic treatment; heavy chronic infection resolves once the worm burden is eradicated.
pitfalls: Misidentifying the eggs as hookworm and misdirecting management
Missing light infections on a single stool sample
Attributing eosinophilia to allergy rather than looking for intestinal helminths
Overlooking the animal reservoir and manure exposure when advising on prevention
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
management: Treat with a benzimidazole anthelmintic such as albendazole or mebendazole, with pyrantel as an alternative, to eradicate the intestinal worm burden
Provide supportive care by correcting iron-deficiency anaemia and supporting nutrition in heavier or chronic infection
Confirm clearance with follow-up stool microscopy, repeating treatment if eggs persist
Screen and treat exposed household or community members in endemic farming settings
Advise prevention through thorough washing or cooking of vegetables and greens, improved sanitation and avoidance of fresh animal manure on crops to interrupt the soil cycle
Seek infectious diseases or tropical medicine input for heavy or diagnostically uncertain infections
